The most important meaning of estimable is: deserving of deep respect, regard, and admiration.

When you describe someone or something as estimable, you are saying that they genuinely deserve to be looked up to — that their qualities, character, or actions make them worthy of being held in high regard by others.

Notice the word hiding inside it: esteem. Esteem means deep respect. So estimable essentially means: capable of being esteemed — or in practice, deserving of that esteem.

Example sentences:

  • "She is an estimable scientist who has spent decades fighting disease."
  • "The judge was known as an estimable man of impeccable fairness and wisdom."
  • "It was an estimable effort from a team that refused to give up."

In all these examples, the word isn't just saying something is "good." It's saying it is genuinely worthy of admiration — something you'd look at with real respect.
A Second, Less Common Meaning: Capable of Being Estimated

"Estimable" can also mean able to be approximately calculated or measured.

  • "The cost of the repairs was estimable once the engineers assessed the damage."

This meaning is mostly found in technical or formal writing. In everyday reading and conversation, if you come across "estimable," it almost certainly means worthy of respect — not this second sense.

"Estimable" is a formal word. You won't hear it in casual conversations. It belongs to written English — literature, formal speeches, tributes, journalism, and academic writing. Using it in a text to a friend would sound stiff, but in a written tribute or a formal review, it fits naturally and elegantly.

• It is not the same as "estimated." "An estimated cost" and "an estimable person" are completely different things.
  • It does not simply mean "good" or "decent." It carries a stronger, more genuine sense of being truly worthy of admiration.
  • It is not a word for mild praise. It suggests real, lasting worthiness — not just a passing compliment.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how a word sits among its neighbors helps you feel its exact weight.

  • Admirable — the closest synonym, and more commonly used. Slightly warmer and more personal in tone than estimable.
  • Respectable — means meeting a standard of decency, but sits lower than estimable. A respectable person is decent; an estimable person is genuinely admirable.
  • Commendable — focuses on praising a specific action. Estimable describes a deeper, broader worthiness — often of a person's whole character or body of work.
  • Honorable — focuses specifically on moral uprightness and integrity.
  • Praiseworthy — very close to estimable, but more straightforward and less formal.

Among all these, estimable carries the most dignified, all-round sense of being worthy of high regard — not for one deed, but as a whole.

If you saw this sentence: "He was an estimable leader whose calm judgment saved the company," — you'd now know it means he was a leader who truly deserved deep respect and admiration, someone whose qualities made him worthy of being held in the highest regard.

It's a word of genuine, measured praise — the kind you'd use when you want to say someone has truly earned their good reputation.
